tiaa-design-system.title: Scaling an enterprise financial design system
tiaa-design-system.summary: Unified fragmented patterns across web and mobile into a governed component system teams could actually adopt.
tiaa-design-system.context: TIAA runs a large set of web and mobile products serving customers, advisors, and internal teams across retirement, banking, and investing. Multiple product groups were designing the same patterns in slightly different ways, which slowed delivery and made the experience feel inconsistent from one product to the next. The design system work set out to give every team a shared, dependable foundation to build on.
tiaa-design-system.problem: Duplicated components and one-off patterns meant teams rebuilt the same buttons, forms, and interaction models over and over. Quality varied, accessibility was uneven, and there was no clear owner for shared patterns. The hard part was not drawing components. It was building a system flexible enough for very different products while keeping enough governance that it did not fragment the moment teams started using it.
responsibilities: Led the design system across web and mobile products as Experience Design Lead
Set component standards, states, and interaction patterns other designers built from
Partnered with designers across product teams to bring their components into a shared, governed system
Partnered with engineering and product leadership on governance, adoption, and roadmap
approach: Audited existing patterns across products to find the real overlaps and the true one-offs
Defined a contribution and ownership model so teams could extend the system without forking it
Documented usage, states, and accessibility expectations so adoption did not depend on a hallway conversation
Built components as reusable, themeable primitives rather than fixed screens
Held accessibility and responsive behavior as requirements, not enhancements
decisions: Defined clear component ownership and a contribution model so shared patterns had a home and did not drift
Invested in documentation and usage guidance early, because a system only helps if people can adopt it without you in the room
Designed components to scale across product teams without fragmenting ownership
Prioritized long-term maintainability over short-term convenience, even when it slowed a single release
designSystem: Component library with defined default, hover, focus, pressed, and disabled states
Interaction patterns and selection models teams could reuse across regulated products
Accessibility baked into component specs so it carried forward automatically
Documentation and governance structure that let the internal team maintain and extend the system
tiaa-design-system.outcome: Delivered a governed, reusable component and interaction-pattern system that teams could adopt and extend, with documentation that let the internal team maintain and grow it after the initial work.
tiaa-design-system.reflection: The interesting challenge here was governance, not visuals. A system that is too rigid gets ignored, and one that is too loose fragments within a quarter. Most of the work was finding that balance and making adoption easy enough that teams chose the system on its merits. It is a good example of how I think about design at scale: fewer, better decisions that hold up as more people build on them.

unitedhealth-transportation.title: Designing accessible transportation benefits for health-plan members
unitedhealth-transportation.summary: Rebuilt a stressful, multi-step scheduling flow into a clear, accessible experience for members booking rides to care.
unitedhealth-transportation.context: Eligible members of certain health plans can schedule transportation to and from medical appointments as a covered benefit. The people using it are often older, managing health conditions, or arranging a ride under time pressure. The experience had to be dependable and easy to trust, because a missed or confusing booking can mean a missed appointment.
unitedhealth-transportation.problem: Scheduling a ride took too many steps and left members unsure whether the booking had actually gone through. In a regulated healthcare product, edge cases and eligibility rules add real complexity, and every added step is another place for someone to get stuck or lose confidence. The challenge was reducing effort and doubt without cutting the details the benefit legitimately requires.
responsibilities: Led product design for the transportation scheduling experience as Principal UI/UX Designer
Designed the end-to-end flow across eligibility, booking, confirmation, and ride status
Ran user research and usability testing to validate the flow with real members
Partnered with product, engineering, and clinical stakeholders inside a regulated environment
approach: Mapped the full scheduling journey to find where members hesitated or dropped off
Ran usability testing to check that each step was understandable under real conditions
Designed clear confirmation and status at every point so members always knew where things stood
Worked through eligibility and edge cases with product and clinical partners so the happy path stayed simple
Held accessibility as a first-class requirement given the member population
decisions: Simplified the scheduling flow to reduce the effort of booking a ride
Made confirmation and status explicit at each step, because certainty matters most when someone is arranging medical care
Limited choices at critical decision points to lower cognitive load without hiding what members needed
Designed for accessibility and edge cases up front rather than retrofitting them
designSystem: Reusable, accessible patterns for scheduling, confirmation, and status that could carry across regulated healthcare flows
Consistent communication patterns so system messages felt like one coherent voice
unitedhealth-transportation.outcome: Delivered a clearer, more accessible scheduling experience that reduced steps, made every booking easy to confirm, and gave members more confidence arranging rides to their appointments.
unitedhealth-transportation.reflection: This project was a reminder that in healthcare, clarity is the feature. People are not admiring the interface; they are trying to get to a doctor. The most valuable decisions were the quiet ones, like confirming a booking clearly and removing a step that added doubt. Designing for members under stress, inside real regulatory constraints, is exactly the kind of complex, high-stakes work I want to keep doing.

nutrient-website.title: Unifying five products into one developer platform
nutrient-website.summary: Consolidated five products and brands into one product-led platform, designed and built with React and Astro.
nutrient-website.context: Nutrient is a document processing and SDK platform used by developers and enterprise teams. The company had grown into five separate product websites and brands, which made the offering hard to understand as one platform. This engagement, delivered through my consultancy Push Refresh, brought those products together into a single product-led site that had to explain genuinely technical capabilities without burying the reader.
nutrient-website.problem: The site had to speak to developers evaluating an SDK and to buyers who needed to understand the platform quickly, without watering down the technical depth either audience relied on. Fragmented content across five brands made it hard to differentiate offerings or guide people to the right place. The structure also had to keep working as the product line expanded.
responsibilities: Led UX and UI for the entire website as Principal Product Designer
Designed and built the site in React and Astro, taking the work from design through production
Partnered with product and marketing to align messaging with what the platform actually does
Owned performance, accessibility, and maintainability as part of the build, not a handoff
approach: Started from a product-first information architecture instead of a marketing-first one
Built reusable layout and content patterns so the team could keep iterating without a redesign
Chose Astro for speed and pulled in React only where interactivity earned it
Designed with implementation in mind and built it myself, which removed most of the usual handoff loss
Treated accessibility and page performance as constraints the design had to satisfy
decisions: Led with a product-first structure so the site explained the platform, not just marketed it
Made clarity the primary constraint and surfaced technical complexity only where it added value
Built reusable patterns so ongoing changes did not require rebuilding pages
Split the stack between Astro and React to keep the site fast while supporting the interactive pieces that needed it
designSystem: Reusable layout and content blocks that let non-designers extend the site safely
A component set shared between design and the production React and Astro build, so what was designed is what shipped
nutrient-website.outcome: Shipped a fast, product-led website that pulls five products into one coherent story and gives the team a base they can keep building on. Because I designed and built it, the work moved from concept to production without losing intent in handoff.
nutrient-website.reflection: This is the kind of project I do best: real product complexity, a systems problem underneath, and design that runs all the way into code. Consolidating five brands into one story took as much editing as designing, deciding what to say plainly and what to leave out. Owning both the design and the front end meant the fast, accessible result on screen was the same thing I had in the file.

images.caption: Navigation was structured around the product line so it could absorb new offerings without a redesign.

lowes-pro-supply.title: Streamlining ordering for professional contractors
lowes-pro-supply.summary: Reduced navigation depth and context switching so contractors could move through repeat ordering tasks with less friction.
lowes-pro-supply.context: Lowe's Pro Supply serves professional contractors who manage inventory, ordering, and fulfillment as part of their day. These are not casual browsers. They work in fast, operational settings and use the same flows repeatedly, so small amounts of friction add up across a shift.
lowes-pro-supply.problem: Common tasks required too much navigation and context switching, which slowed people down on work they do constantly. The challenge was simplifying operational flows without stripping out the flexibility professional users need for varied, real-world situations.
responsibilities: Designed core application workflows for professional, task-focused users
Focused the interface on repeat, operational use rather than first-time discovery
Worked within product and engineering constraints on feasibility and scope
approach: Focused on the repeat tasks contractors run most, not one-time onboarding moments
Consolidated related actions into focused views to cut navigation depth
Prioritized speed and scannability so the interface kept up with operational pace
Kept patterns consistent across workflows to reduce training and cognitive overhead
decisions: Consolidated related actions into focused views to reduce navigation depth
Prioritized speed and scannability over visual detail, because the interface is used repeatedly, not admired
Designed for repeat workflows rather than first-time discovery
Held patterns consistent across the app so people did not relearn the interface screen to screen
lowes-pro-supply.outcome: Focused the core ordering and account flows on speed, consistency, and repeat use, so professional users could move through routine tasks with less friction.
lowes-pro-supply.reflection: Designing for professionals who use a tool all day is a different discipline than designing for first impressions. The value is in small time savings on tasks people repeat constantly, which means restraint and consistency matter more than novelty. It is a good example of designing for the actual context of use rather than the demo.

images.alt: Access and onboarding screens for the Lowe's Pro Supply application
images.caption: Onboarding was kept lightweight so professional users could get to their actual work quickly.

images.alt: Dashboard, pro tools, and account management views
images.caption: Related account and pro tools were grouped into focused views to reduce the navigation cost of routine tasks.
Search and discovery were tuned for speed and scannability, since finding the right item fast is the core repeat task.

synquery-product.title: Defining an expert-network product from the ground up
synquery-product.summary: Defined the core product and shipped the marketing site for an early-stage expert-network platform, working directly with the founders.
synquery-product.context: Synquery is an early-stage expert network platform that connects organizations with specialized expertise. Delivered through Push Refresh, the work covered both the core product experience and the public marketing site. Early-stage work like this rewards judgment about what to build now and what to leave room for later.
synquery-product.problem: A new product needs to feel clear and credible without overbuilding for a scale it has not reached. The challenge was defining foundations strong enough to trust, but flexible enough to evolve as the product and the company learned what mattered.
responsibilities: Led product UX and UI for the core platform as Principal Product Designer
Designed and developed the marketing website end to end
Worked directly with the founders on product definition and positioning
Balanced speed, clarity, and scalability in early-stage decisions
approach: Focused on the core workflows that had to work well before anything else
Designed flexible patterns that could grow without a rebuild
Kept product and website design aligned so the story was consistent everywhere
Partnered closely with founders to turn an early vision into concrete decisions
decisions: Prioritized core workflows over edge-case features so the first release was focused
Designed flexible patterns that could scale without rework
Aligned the product and website so they told one coherent story
Chose clarity over feature density, which matters more when a product is still earning trust
synquery-product.outcome: Delivered a cohesive product and web experience that gave Synquery clear foundations to launch from while leaving room to iterate quickly as the platform matured.
synquery-product.reflection: Early-stage design is mostly about judgment: knowing what deserves real structure now and what should stay loose. Working directly with founders meant moving fast without losing the thread between product decisions and how the company talked about itself. Doing both the product and the site kept that story consistent from the first screen to the homepage.
